subject: dermatology
title: Impetigo Contagiosa

steps.tx: **Impetigo contagiosa** represents the non-bullous, highly contagious superficial pyoderma caused primarily by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. Lesions begin as transient, thin-walled vesicles on an erythematous base around the perioral and periorbital regions of young children. Rapid vesicle rupture releases seropurulent exudate that desiccates into thick, golden, honey-coloured crusts adherent to the underlying erosion. Gentle removal of the crust reveals a moist, weeping base that re-crusts quickly without residual scarring.
steps.say: Non-bullous impetigo is a superficial skin infection marked by fragile vesicles that rupture and form characteristic honey-coloured crusts around the mouth and nose. It heals without deep scarring because inflammation is confined to the subcorneal space.

vis.alt: Clinical photograph of impetigo demonstrating superficial blistering and crusting.
vis.caption: Erythematous superficial eroded plaques with characteristic honey-coloured crusting on facial skin. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Bullous impetigo** occurs almost exclusively as a consequence of localized infection by phage group II Staphylococcus aureus strains, specifically types 71 and 55. These bacteria produce exfoliative toxins A and B, which act as serine proteases selectively cleaving desmoglein-1 in the superficial stratum granulosum. Patients present with large, flaccid bullae containing clear yellow fluid that turns turbid. Unlike non-bullous impetigo, these bullae frequently involve the trunk and intertriginous folds, leaving a delicate collarette of scale upon rupture.
steps.say: Bullous impetigo results from staphylococcal exfoliative toxins that cleave desmoglein-1 high in the epidermis. Flaccid blisters expand and collapse, leaving thin collarettes of scale across the trunk and diaper area.

left.title: Non-Bullous Impetigo
points: Mixed Staph aureus and Strep pyogenes

right.title: Bullous Impetigo
points: Flaccid bullae with collarettes of scale

steps.tx: **Ecthyma** is a deep, ulcerative variant of impetigo that penetrates fully through the epidermis into the underlying dermis, typically provoked by Streptococcus pyogenes in neglected or immunocompromised individuals. Lesions arise preferentially on the lower extremities, initiating as vesicles that rapidly ulcerate into punched-out, painful circular sores with raised, indurated, violaceous borders. The base is covered by an adherent, thick, hard, greenish-yellow crust. Because dermal collagen is destroyed, ecthyma invariably heals with permanent depressed scarring.
steps.say: Ecthyma is a deep-seated streptococcal ulcer that penetrates through the dermis, unlike superficial impetigo. It presents on the legs as punched-out sores covered by thick black-brown crusts that heal with permanent scars.

vis.title: Invasion Depth in Staphylococcal and Streptococcal Pyodermas

steps.tx: **Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis** is an immune-complex renal complication that can follow streptococcal impetigo after a latent period of three to six weeks. Nephritogenic strains of Streptococcus pyogenes, particularly M types 49, 55, 57, and 60, deposit cationic streptococcal antigens on glomerular basement membranes. Early systemic antibiotic eradication of skin streptococci does not reliably prevent glomerulonephritis. Importantly, acute rheumatic fever does not occur following cutaneous streptococcal infections, distinguishing impetigo from streptococcal pharyngitis.
steps.say: Glomerulonephritis can develop several weeks after streptococcal impetigo, triggered by specific nephritogenic M types. Remember an essential exam fact: acute rheumatic fever never follows skin streptococcal infections, only throat infections.

vis.title: Post-Streptococcal Sequelae by Infection Site
rows: Antibiotics do not reliably prevent PSGN

steps.tx: **Mupirocin** two percent topical ointment or cream provides first-line antimicrobial therapy for localized, uncomplicated impetigo contagiosa with limited lesions. Derived from Pseudomonas fluorescens, mupirocin selectively binds and inhibits bacterial isoleucyl-transfer RNA synthetase, terminating protein synthesis in Gram-positive cocci including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. The ointment is applied three times daily for five to seven days after gently soaking and removing adherent honey-coloured crusts with warm water compresses to maximize drug penetration into the raw base.
steps.say: Topical two percent mupirocin is the drug of choice for localized impetigo. It halts bacterial protein synthesis by blocking isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase. Always instruct parents to soak and soften crusts before applying the ointment.

left.title: Topical Therapy Indications
points: Mupirocin or retapamulin for 5 to 7 days

right.title: Systemic Therapy Indications
points: Presence of fever or systemic illness

steps.tx: **Cephalexin** or oral amoxicillin-clavulanate represents the standard systemic antibiotic regimen for widespread impetigo, multiple active lesions, or cases accompanied by fever and lymphadenopathy. Treatment is maintained for seven days to ensure clinical cure and suppress transmission within households and schools. For confirmed or strongly suspected community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, oral clindamycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or linezolid should be selected according to local antimicrobial susceptibility profiles.
steps.say: Systemic oral antibiotics like cephalexin or co-amoxiclav are necessary when impetigo is widespread or involves fever. For suspected MRSA, switch to oral clindamycin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole based on sensitivity testing.

nodes.label: Household Hygiene
nodes.sub: Separate towels, trim nails, treat nasal carriers

steps.tx: **Anti-DNase B** antibody testing provides the most dependable serological evidence of preceding cutaneous streptococcal infection when evaluating suspected post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. In skin pyodermas, antistreptolysin O titres frequently fail to rise because skin surface lipids and cholesterol bind and inactivate streptolysin O, neutralizing its antigenicity. In contrast, anti-DNase B titres rise in over ninety percent of cutaneous streptococcal infections, peaking six to eight weeks after initial inoculation.
steps.say: When investigating kidney disease after skin sores, request anti-DNase B rather than ASO titres. Skin lipids neutralize streptolysin O antigenicity, leaving ASO falsely negative in over half of impetigo cases.

steps.tx: **Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome** arises from haematogenous dissemination of exfoliative toxins A or B from an occult focal staphylococcal infection, such as purulent conjunctivitis or omphalitis. Unlike bullous impetigo where bacteria colonize the bullae, the widespread flaccid blisters and sheets of epidermal denudation in this syndrome are completely sterile. Gentle lateral sliding pressure on perilesional normal-appearing skin produces epidermal separation, demonstrating a positive Nikolsky sign.
steps.say: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome results from circulating exfoliative toxins spreading from a distant focus. The generalized blisters are sterile, and gentle lateral skin pressure produces positive Nikolsky peeling.
